title: Is It Wrong to Live Together Before Marriage?
excerpt: Many couples live together first out of caution, not carelessness, and their reasons deserve a hearing. Scripture's answer begins with what marriage is: a public covenant made before God and witnesses, with the body's promise kept inside it.
body:
A couple in their late twenties signed a lease together last spring. They split the rent, share a dog, and have talked about marriage the way people talk about buying a house, as something they will certainly do once things settle down. Her parents divorced when she was nine, and she remembers the two Christmases and the custody calendar on the refrigerator. She would rather find out now than learn it the way her mother did. A young man in another city is engaged and living with his fiancée, and he has stopped going to church because he assumes he knows what the pastor would say. A grandmother in a third town prays every night for a granddaughter who lives with a boyfriend, and she has never once asked the girl how she's doing, because she doesn't know how to start the conversation without sounding as though she were passing sentence on a life she loves.

The skeptic watching all this has a fair point to make. The church, he says, treats a piece of paper from the county clerk as if it were a sacrament. Two people who have loved each other faithfully for five years are called sinners, while a couple who married at nineteen and fought for fifteen years are honored for staying together. And the Bible, he adds, never mentions a marriage license at all.

He's right about the license. He is right, too, that the church has often spoken to couples who live together with more heat than understanding. This essay tries to do better than that, which means stating the couple's own case properly before saying anything else. It also means being plain about where the historic Christian faith stands, because pretending it has no view would not be kind to anyone.

The site's page for couples deciding [whether to get married](/help/dating) puts the church's teaching in one sentence, and then, in the next breath, says what comes after it: "If you've already crossed that line, you aren't ruined or second-rate." Its advice for those already sharing a home is short: "If you live together, talk honestly with a pastor about faithfulness from here." That is where this essay is headed too. And if the person you live with frightens you, controls you, or keeps you from friends and family, the question in this essay can wait. The same page lists the National Domestic Violence Hotline, and [Find Help](/help) has the rest.

## The Case for Living Together First

Most couples who move in together aren't rejecting marriage. Many of them want it badly, and that is part of why they hesitate. A great many grew up inside a divorce, and they watched promises made in white dresses and rented tuxedos come apart in lawyers' offices. They concluded, reasonably, that a ceremony doesn't hold a marriage together, and that it would be foolish to promise forever to someone you haven't lived with through a winter, a layoff, a stomach virus and an argument about dishes. Living together, on this view, is not a lack of seriousness. It's a form of caution.

There's also money. Rent in most cities is high enough that two incomes under one roof can be the difference between saving and drowning. Weddings have become expensive productions, and couples who can't afford the production often decide to wait until they can, while life goes on. Some couples feel that the license is a government form, that the state's interest in their love is mostly about taxes and insurance, and that what makes them married in any meaningful sense is the commitment they've already made to each other in private.

And many of these couples love each other well. They are faithful, they share what they have, they care for each other's parents, and they would be hurt to hear their home described as anything less than a family. Some of them are more tender with one another than couples who married in church.

Some of this has to be granted without reluctance. The fear of divorce is not foolish; it comes from real wounds. The ceremony is not the marriage. And love that is patient and faithful is good wherever it is found. A Christian who can't say those things has not yet understood the couple he wants to talk to.

But the case for living together first rests on an assumption that deserves to be looked at, which is that marriage is mainly a private arrangement between two people, and that the public part, the vows and the witnesses and the name of God, is decoration on top of it. That assumption is exactly where Scripture disagrees.

## What Marriage Is in Scripture

The Bible's first word about marriage comes before there is any state, any license or any church. "Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh" (Genesis 2:24). The verse has three movements, and the order matters. A man leaves one household, publicly, in a world where a household was everyone's business. He holds fast, which is the language of loyalty and covenant. And then the two become one flesh. The joining of bodies comes last, inside the leaving and the holding fast, not before them. The Study Bible's summary of [Genesis 2](/study/bible/genesis/2) says the chapter "closes with the first marriage and a couple naked and unashamed." The nakedness without shame belongs to the end of that sequence.

Marriage in Israel was a covenant, a binding promise made before God with consequences for everyone around it. The prophet Malachi rebuked men who were walking away from their wives, and the reason he gives is striking: "Because the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant" (Malachi 2:14). The note on [Malachi 2](/study/bible/malachi/2) describes "the covenant of marriage that God himself witnesses." God stands at a wedding as a witness. That is why Proverbs can describe an unfaithful wife as one who "forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God" (Proverbs 2:17). The promise is made to a person and before God at the same time.

The community witnessed it too. When Boaz married Ruth, he did it at the city gate in front of the elders, and the whole scene turns on a public word: "You are witnesses this day" (Ruth 4:9). The people answered, "We are witnesses" (Ruth 4:11). Jesus himself went to a wedding feast at Cana, a public celebration crowded enough that the wine ran out, and he kept it going (John 2:1-11). In Scripture a marriage is never only two people deciding something in a kitchen. It is a promise made where others can hear it, so that others can hold you to it.

The New Testament then says the most remarkable thing about it. After quoting Genesis 2:24, Paul writes, "This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church" (Ephesians 5:32). Marriage is a picture of a love that binds itself publicly and permanently to its beloved, the way Christ bound himself to his people at the cost of his life. A covenant that God witnesses, that a community hears, and that reflects the faithfulness of Christ can't be reduced to paperwork, but it also can't be reduced to a private feeling.

## Why the Body Belongs Inside the Promise

This is the ground on which every major Christian tradition, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, has taught that sexual union belongs within marriage. The teaching is old and it is shared, and it isn't a quirk of American evangelicals. "Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled," says the letter to the Hebrews (Hebrews 13:4). The dating page quotes that verse and then says plainly, "I won't blur it." Neither will this essay.

But the reason matters more than the rule, and the reason is not that the body is shameful. The Song of Songs celebrates desire without embarrassment, and it still repeats a refrain: "that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases" (Song of Songs 2:7). Paul's argument in 1 Corinthians 6 is about the body's dignity, not its dirtiness. "Flee from sexual immorality," he writes, and then gives the reason: "Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body" (1 Corinthians 6:18-20). The note on [1 Corinthians 6](/study/bible/1-corinthians/6) says Paul was answering slogans "that treated the body as unimportant." The sexual union says with the body what the vows say with the mouth: all of me, for all of my life. When the body says it before the mouth has, the body is making a promise the couple has carefully not made.

That is the real tension in living together before marriage. The couple shares a bed, a budget, a lease and often a future, and yet the whole point of the arrangement, for many of them, is that they have kept a way out. They are giving each other nearly everything except the promise. Scott Stanley, a psychologist at the University of Denver who has spent many years studying couples, has a phrase for how this often happens: many couples don't decide to live together so much as slide into it, one toothbrush and one weekend at a time, and then find that leaving has become hard before staying has ever been chosen. Sliding is not deciding. The Christian vision of marriage asks for the deciding first.

## How the Church Learned to Insist on Witnesses

It helps to know that the church did not always require a ceremony, and that the history runs the opposite way from what the skeptic might expect. For much of the medieval period, the Western church held that a marriage was made by the free consent of the two people, and a promise exchanged privately, without priest or witness, could be counted a valid marriage. These were called clandestine marriages, and they caused enormous suffering. A man could promise marriage in private, take what he wanted, and later deny that any promise had been made. With no witness there was no proof, and the one left without a home, a name or support for a child was almost always the woman.

So the church moved, step by step, to make marriage public. In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council required that coming marriages be announced in church beforehand, the practice later known as reading the banns. In 1563 the Council of Trent, in a decree known by its first word, Tametsi, required Catholics to marry before a priest and witnesses. In England, Lord Hardwicke's Marriage Act of 1753 did something similar under the law of the land. Protestant churches insisted on public weddings too. Whatever else one thinks of these institutions, the pressure toward a public ceremony grew largely out of the need to protect the weaker party from a promise made in the dark.

That history reframes the license. The state's paperwork is a late and partial echo of something older and more important: a marriage should be visible, so that the promise can be held to by others. When a couple says the license is just paper, they are right that paper doesn't make a marriage. But a public promise was never about paper. It was about not leaving the person you love without a witness.

## Where We Have Failed

None of that gives the church permission to speak to cohabiting couples the way it often has. Many of us have treated sexual sin as worse than every other kind, and living together as the most visible kind of all, while quietly tolerating gluttony, greed, contempt for the poor and cruelty in our own marriages. We have sometimes made weddings so expensive and so focused on the show that a couple who couldn't afford the show felt they couldn't afford to marry. We have preached about the sanctity of marriage and then offered almost nothing to help people prepare for it, or to help married couples who were falling apart. And many of us have shamed couples so effectively that the only thing they learned was to stop coming to church, which is exactly where they might have found help.

Some of the couples who live together are children of marriages that the church blessed and then watched fail. Their caution is partly our failure. A church that wants to speak credibly about the covenant of marriage has to keep its own covenants, and has to care as much about the marriages inside its walls as about the arrangements outside them.

Jesus did not avoid this subject. At a well in Samaria he told a woman the truth about her life: "for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband" (John 4:18). He said it plainly, without pretending her situation was fine. But he said it in the middle of a conversation he had started, having asked her for a drink when no respectable man would have spoken to her, and he went on to offer her living water. She ran back to her town to tell everyone about him. The truth was not softened, and she did not leave the conversation crushed.

## If You Are Already Living Together

If this describes your life, a few things can be said to you directly.

You are not beyond God's reach, and you are not a second-class Christian. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9). That promise is for you exactly as it is for everyone else.

Repentance here doesn't have to mean drama. It means turning toward what God calls good, and for most couples that takes one of two shapes. Some will realize that they already intend to marry, that the only thing between them and a public promise is fear, money or a guest list, and that the faithful step is to marry, simply and soon. A small wedding with a pastor, two witnesses and a dinner afterward is a real wedding. Others will realize that they are not ready to make that promise, or are not sure they should make it to this person, and for them the faithful step may be to live apart while they decide. Neither of those is easy, and neither should be taken alone.

That's where a pastor comes in. Most pastors have had this conversation many times, and a good one will not be shocked or cold. Ask for a meeting, tell the truth about your situation, and ask for help thinking through the next step. If there are children, finances or leases involved, a pastor can help you work out an honest path that doesn't treat those things lightly. If you have been away from church because you assumed you knew what would be said, it may surprise you how much of the conversation is about your future rather than your past.

And if you are the parent or the grandmother, the first step is probably not a speech. It's asking the people you love how they are, inviting them to dinner, and earning the right to say the truth by first showing that you will still be there after you've said it. The father in Jesus' parable "saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him" (Luke 15:20) before the son had finished his apology.

## The Promise Worth Making

The fear underneath so much cohabitation is a fear of being trapped in a promise that can't be kept. That fear has been earned in a great many families, and it deserves compassion. But the answer Scripture gives is not to avoid promising. It is to make the promise in the presence of the God who keeps his.

Every Christian wedding is a small rehearsal of a larger one. The church is called the bride of Christ because he did not test the relationship first. He bound himself to people who had given him every reason to keep a way out, and he made his vow in public, on a cross outside a city gate, where everyone could see. The couple who stands before God and a few witnesses and says "until death" isn't claiming to be strong enough to keep that promise alone. They are placing their small vow inside his large one.

The couple with the lease and the dog may marry next year or may not. The young man may come back to church or may not. The grandmother may find the words. Scripture does not promise any of them an easy road. It does offer them something better than a trial run: a God who witnesses promises, keeps his own, and does not leave the people he loves without a witness.

*"Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled."* (Hebrews 13:4)

*"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh."* (Genesis 2:24)
